overview: The Medford School Committee is the governing body responsible for setting educational policies, approving district budgets, and overseeing the operations and leadership of Medford Public Schools. The archive documents 62 meetings of the committee spanning from September 2024 through October 2026. Over this timeframe, the committee guided a superintendent leadership transition, advanced feasibility and design planning for a new comprehensive high school with the Massachusetts School Building Authority, funded extensive HVAC replacements across multiple campuses, and revised graduation requirements following changes to state MCAS mandates. The body also worked to address elementary school overcrowding, expand childcare capacity, and resolve regional student transportation constraints. At its most recent meeting in October 2026, the committee reviewed strategic planning survey results and considered a draft elementary school reassignment policy.

threads.name: Medford High School building project
threads.summary: The committee advanced through the Massachusetts School Building Authority (MSBA) process to design a new or renovated Medford Comprehensive High School, establishing an initial enrollment capacity target of 1,395 students and hiring Left Field as Owner's Project Manager (M19#7, M20#2, M20#4, M27#5). The committee eliminated Medford Square and Columbus Park from consideration to focus on the existing campus, navigating historical Department of Conservation and Recreation deed restrictions on Edgerly Field that influenced schematic options (M32#6, M51#7, M54#3). The committee approved the project's educational plan, selected a Construction Manager at Risk delivery method, and established LEED Silver sustainability goals (M44#3, M46#6, M58#7). The committee also approved updated Chapter 74 vocational viability filings and restructured building committee membership for the schematic design phase (M57#1, M59#9).

threads.name: Superintendent leadership transition
threads.summary: Following contract discussions in executive session, the committee accepted the resignation of Superintendent Dr. Marice Edouard-Vincent after seven years of service and appointed Assistant Superintendent Dr. Suzanne Galusi as Interim Superintendent (M04#1, M14#2, M16#9). After reviewing conflict of interest disclosures, the committee authorized Dr. Galusi to lead collective bargaining and monitored her transition through entry findings and performance evaluations (M18#1, M35#13, M38#5, M43#6). In February 2026, the committee voted to appoint Dr. Galusi as permanent superintendent rather than conduct an external search (M44#4). The committee subsequently approved a three-year contract, adjusted the evaluation cadence to match the school year, and approved her annual performance goals for the 2026-2027 school year (M50#6, M56#11, M60#6).

threads.name: School facilities and HVAC capital upgrades
threads.summary: To address aging mechanical infrastructure, the committee authorized immediate boiler and water heater replacements before initiating district-wide HVAC upgrades using construction management at risk (M01#9, M06#6, M11#6). The committee recommended an initial $5 million bond and later approved a $25.775 million bond for comprehensive HVAC and roof replacements at the McGlynn and Andrews schools, followed by an approved solar power purchase agreement (M15#6, M24#7, M40#4). A comprehensive assessment identified $83.7 million in needed repairs across five schools, prompting revisions to the capital plan for alignment with city planning standards (M38#3, M41#6, M46#7). For Roberts Elementary School, the committee submitted MSBA repair statements, selected an air-to-water heat pump model, and approved a $22.7 million schematic design for HVAC electrification and roof replacement (M22#1, M56#5, M59#4).

threads.name: Elementary capacity and grade restructuring
threads.summary: Persistent overcrowding at Roberts Elementary School prompted early calls from staff for comprehensive redistricting and facility space adjustments (M01#8, M02#6, M25#4). In response, the committee relocated preschool classrooms from Roberts to Missituk Elementary and formed a space planning task force to study enrollment balances (M30#6, M30#7). The committee evaluated an architectural space study and surveyed the community regarding middle school reconfiguration models that would reorganize grades into K-4 and 5-8 structures (M39#5, M40#5). In July 2026, the committee voted to delay any middle school grade configuration changes until the 2028-2029 school year, and later began reviewing a formal elementary school reassignment policy (M58#4, M62#5).

threads.name: Graduation requirements and MCAS policy revisions
threads.summary: Following voter approval of state ballot Question 2 eliminating the MCAS graduation requirement, the committee updated Policy IKF to replace the state testing determination with successful completion of aligned courses in English, math, and science (M03#8, M19#3, M21#7). The committee refined graduation rules to clarify math pathways, ensure graduation ceremony participation for students completing special education certificates of completion, and expand elective options for physical education and health (M24#6, M25#3, M30#4). The committee rescinded the obsolete Policy IKFC-MCAS and piloted a late-entry flex schedule for non-testing students during spring testing sessions (M31#9, M47#4). A subsequent resolution directed subcommittees to examine district alignment with emerging state graduation council frameworks (M58#9).

threads.name: Student transportation operations and safety
threads.summary: Regional driver shortages through vendor Eastern Bus caused acute route disruptions, middle school rider eligibility reviews, and bus overcrowding early in the term (M01#12, M02#8, M07#4). To secure long-term service, the committee approved a new five-year yellow bus contract with Eastern Bus while referring an electrification feasibility study to subcommittee (M31#4). The committee passed a resolution requesting that the City Council authorize automated stop-arm camera enforcement and approved plans to deploy internal paraprofessionals as bus monitors (M34#8, M36#5, M37#6). In autumn 2026, the committee introduced high school late bus routes to support students participating in after-school programming (M62#4).

threads.name: Childcare and after-school programming expansion
threads.summary: Confronted by lengthy waitlists for district childcare, the committee requested administrative reviews of program capacity, staff ratios, and transportation barriers (M06#8, M11#3). The committee adjusted tuition rates, introduced an early 4:00 p.m. pickup option to free up slots, and engaged the Belmont After School Enrichment Collaborative (BASIC) to conduct a program review (M25#1, M28#2, M31#5). Following BASIC's recommendations, the committee approved an expansion plan adding 150 student seats, created full-time site director positions, and established a revised multi-day rate card (M33#3, M50#4, M50#5). By September 2026, the administration reported a 68 percent reduction in the after-school program waitlist (M60#5).
